sections.html:
Centennial is a home rule city in Arapahoe County, just south of Denver. Interstate 25 splits it roughly in half, with most business and entertainment centers on the west side. The elevation is 5,722 feet.

It had 108,418 residents in the 2020 census, the 11th largest municipality in Colorado. Estimates since then are 108,853 for 2024 and 108,658 for July 1, 2025, which describes a settled city more than a booming one. Voters created it on February 7, 2001, and approved home rule in 2008.

One detail matters before any sale: Arapahoe County, not the city, bills and collects your property tax. County offices count as much as city hall.

sections.h2: Who issues permits on your street
sections.html:
Some nearby land is unincorporated county ground, including Dove Valley and the land under Centennial Airport. The airport sits next to the city, not inside it, and was operating more than 30 years before the city existed. Which jurisdiction covers your street decides who issues permits and enforces code, so confirm that before you start repairs.

If your house is close to the airport or the interstate, tell buyers up front. An inspector or a neighbor will mention the noise anyway.

Roof situationWhat the city requires
Repair over 100 square feetMajor repair, permit needed
Smaller repairNo permit
Repairs above 25 percent of the roof areaComplete tear off and reroof
Every reroof permitMid-roof inspection, which may be done by photo
  • Work must meet the 2021 International Residential Code.
  • A replacement strips every existing layer of roof covering down to the deck.
  • Drip edge goes on all roof edges, and an ice barrier underlayment goes on all roofs.
  • Used or harvested materials are not allowed.

Age and storm damage push owners toward roof work, and these rules change what it costs and how long it takes. The city's residential roof page has the full list. A buyer who takes the house as is inherits that job instead of you.

sections.h2: How Arapahoe County handles property tax
sections.html:
The Arapahoe County Treasurer collects tax on Centennial homes and passes it to the county, school districts and other local governments. Residential property uses two assessment rates: 6.25 percent for local government and 7.05 percent for schools.

  • Senior and military deferral applications run from January 1 through April 1.
  • The Treasurer handles Certificate of Taxes Due requests for individuals and for title companies.
  • Excess foreclosure funds go through the Public Trustee.

For payment dates and questions, call the Treasurer's Office at 303-795-4550 or visit the Arapahoe County Treasurer page.

Run the rules against your own roof first. If the damage reaches past 25 percent of the roof area, the city wants a complete tear off, so a patch that looked like a weekend job turns into a full replacement. That means a permit, a removal of every layer down to the deck, new drip edge, an ice barrier underlayment and a mid-roof inspection.

Owners who are short on money, time or both often decide the work is not worth starting. A buyer who purchases the house as is takes on the roof and prices it in, and you skip the permit and inspection steps entirely. If you do reroof, keep the permit paperwork, since it shows the work was inspected.

sections.h2: The Treasurer's role in a sale
sections.html:
When a Centennial house sells, the title company contacts the Arapahoe County Treasurer for a Certificate of Taxes Due. It confirms what is owed on the parcel so the balance can be paid from the closing funds. You can ask for the same document yourself if you want to see the number first.

Owners who qualify for a senior or military deferral should mention it to the title company. The application window runs January 1 through April 1, and the Treasurer can tell you how a deferral fits with a sale.

sections.h2: Weighing a listing against a quick sale
sections.html:
A well-kept house in a settled city can do well on the market. Time is the cost. You prepare the house, host showings, wait on a buyer's inspection and then wait again on a loan. Any repair request after the inspection reopens the price.

A quick as-is sale is the better match when the roof is old, a system is failing, or you have a date that cannot move. Ask for the offer in writing, see what it nets after the tax payoff, and compare that number with a realistic listing price minus repairs and months of carrying costs.

sections.h2: Which school district am I in?
sections.html: Cherry Creek Public Schools covers most of Centennial, and Littleton Public Schools covers the western part. The district line cuts through the city, so your address decides which one applies. Check before you tell a buyer.

sections.h2: Questions buyers ask about a Centennial street
sections.html:
Expect four questions early. Which county bills the tax? Which school district is it? Is the house close to the airport or the interstate? Was the roof ever replaced under a permit? Having the answers written on one page makes you look prepared and speeds up any negotiation. It also saves you from guessing out loud when a buyer's agent calls with a question.

For the first, the answer is Arapahoe County. For the second, it is Cherry Creek Public Schools in most of the city and Littleton Public Schools in the western part. The last two depend on your own records, so dig out the permit file before you list.

sections.h2: What do Centennial sellers usually face?
sections.html:
The typical seller has a well-placed house that needs updating and not much time. Common cases:

  • an inherited house whose heirs live too far away to manage it
  • a roof or major system that needs work before a buyer's inspection
  • a move tied to an employer or a divorce
  • a tenant who has to be dealt with

A direct cash purchase takes the place of the lender and the appraisal, and you pick the closing day. Listing remains an option if it suits you better. Either way, the title company can supply the payoff and tax numbers.

sections.h2: The steps in a Centennial cash sale
sections.html:
1. Send us the address and tell us about the house.
  2. We review it and write an offer for the property as it stands.
  3. A title company confirms the Arapahoe County tax status and looks for liens.
  4. You choose a closing date, sign, and receive the agreed proceeds.

Set the offer next to a listing before deciding. Declining costs nothing.

Before the title company calls, locate your latest tax statement, mortgage payoff details if you have a loan, and any permit records for past roof or system work. If roof repairs were done, those records show what was permitted and inspected, and buyers like to see them.

faqs.q: What county is Centennial, CO in?
faqs.a: Centennial is in Arapahoe County, which bills and collects the property tax.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to replace a roof in Centennial?
faqs.a: Yes, for a major repair or a replacement. Repairs under 100 square feet are small and need no permit, and larger work requires one.

faqs.q: Who handles the Certificate of Taxes Due in Arapahoe County?
faqs.a: The Arapahoe County Treasurer handles those requests for individuals and for title companies. Your title company will normally order it for a sale.

faqs.q: Is Centennial Airport inside the city?
faqs.a: No. It is next to the city on unincorporated Arapahoe County land, and it was in place more than 30 years before the city was incorporated.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Centennial house with an old roof?
faqs.a: Yes. A cash buyer purchases as is, so you do not need to replace the roof before closing. Ask for the offer in writing.
